headline: Tesla says its Optimus humanoid robot now learns household and factory chores mostly by watching first-person videos of people instead of being remotely steered.
score_reason: Pool score kept: a notable claim on how humanoids are trained, but it is Tesla's own, relayed second-hand, with no success rates published.
importance_line: If it holds, robots could learn from large amounts of ordinary video instead of slow remote control, which could speed up when they reach homes and factories, but the claim is Tesla's own, is reported second-hand and comes without success rates.
source: Startup Fortune, citing Drive Tesla Canada and eWeek
summary: Startup Fortune reports, citing Drive Tesla Canada and eWeek, that Tesla's Optimus AI team says one trained network, built mainly on first-person footage of people filmed with helmet-and-backpack cameras, now lets the humanoid robot vacuum a room, stir food, take out the trash and sort car parts without a person steering each move. The outlet notes that Tesla has not published failure rates or success percentages, and that Tesla's reported next step, training on ordinary internet video, is not yet part of today's system.
notes: Read from the pre-fetched full text. Startup Fortune cites driveteslacanada.ca and eWeek; neither was found, and the original Tesla post was not found, so the chain is unclear and both are named. The date of Tesla's statement is not given.
